title: Held together by water: membrane structure and fluidity

objectives.statement: Predict the direction in which a stated change to hydrocarbon chain length, cis unsaturation, cholesterol content, or temperature moves a membrane's fluidity, give the packing or thermal mechanism behind each prediction, and identify the case where the direction depends on the starting state.

Compute how long a lipid takes to diffuse a stated distance in the plane of a membrane from a stated diffusion coefficient, compare that time with the time scale of movement between the two leaflets, and use the comparison to justify describing a membrane as a two-dimensional fluid while naming the idealisation the calculation assumes.

Account for the different lipid and protein composition of an enterocyte's apical and basolateral membranes, and of a membrane's two leaflets, by naming the mechanism that maintains each separation, the observation that demonstrates it, and the limit of what that observation can show.

scenes.title: The lumen is on the other side of five nanometres
scenes.contentHtml:
The lumen is on the other side of five nanometres

Conventional light microscopy separates detail down to about 250 nanometres across the specimen. The boundary that makes a crypt cell a cell is about 5 nanometres thick, fifty times finer than that. Anyone who draws a cell outline from a light micrograph is drawing a line finer than the instrument can resolve, and what that line is made of has to be argued from chemistry and from measurements taken by other means.

Five nanometres is two molecules thick. Two facing layers of lipid, and on the far side of them, in the gut, the lumen.

The word membrane arrives from ordinary English already meaning something, and the ordinary meaning is not wrong so much as thin. A drum skin is a membrane; so is the film inside an eggshell. All of them are sheets that separate one space from another, which is the part biology keeps. From here on the word carries three things the everyday sense does not: the sheet is exactly two molecules of lipid thick, it behaves as a liquid within its own plane, and it decides what crosses it. The plasma membrane is the one enclosing the whole cell, which is the membrane this lesson is about.

What this lesson assumes, and where it comes from

In the course graph this outcome sits downstream of Lipids and membranes (PREM-09.05), which is where lipid chemistry is taught. No lesson has been written for that outcome yet. What follows therefore carries its own short version and does not build a phospholipid from first principles; when PREM-09.05 exists, read it first and this section becomes a reminder.

Three things are assumed. A phospholipid has a water-attracting head containing a phosphate group and two water-avoiding hydrocarbon tails, which makes one molecule with two incompatible halves. A tail is saturated when every carbon-to-carbon bond along it is single, and unsaturated when it carries one or more double bonds; a cis double bond puts a permanent kink in the chain. Cholesterol is a small, rigid, largely water-avoiding molecule carrying a single hydroxyl group at one end. Nothing later in this lesson needs more lipid chemistry than those three sentences.

Nothing holds one lipid to the next

There is no bond between neighbouring phospholipids in a membrane. The sheet is held together by the water on either side of it.

A water-avoiding molecule placed in water forces the surrounding water molecules to reorganise into ordered cage-like arrangements, and forming those cages costs free energy. The cost falls when the water-avoiding parts cluster together, because clustering leaves the smallest number of water molecules affected. Phospholipids therefore aggregate without being told to, tails buried inward and heads exposed to water, and a bilayer is the shape that aggregation takes for a molecule with a bulky head and two tails.

Three consequences follow, and between them they are most of what a membrane can do.

A bilayer cannot have an edge. A free edge exposes buried tails to water, which is the arrangement the whole assembly is avoiding. The only way to have no edge is to close on itself and form a sealed compartment. A cell is a bag because a flat square of bilayer is not a stable object.

A bilayer repairs itself. A small tear creates that same free edge, so the lipids rearrange spontaneously to remove it. No signal, no enzyme and no repair programme is involved. The hole closes because an open hole is the expensive state.

A bilayer can be taken apart and put back together. Pinching a vesicle off one membrane and fusing it into another leaves nothing broken, because there was no bonded lattice to break. Vesicular transport in lesson 05 depends on that.

What else is in there

Lipid is not the bulk of the membrane by mass. Protein accounts for about half the mass of a typical plasma membrane, dropping below a quarter in the myelin that insulates axons and rising to about three quarters in the inner membranes of mitochondria. Read those three figures next to what each membrane does: the one whose main job is electrical insulation carries the least protein, and the one running ATP production carries the most.

The lipid itself is not one substance either. Sterols alone can be up to 40 per cent of the total lipid in a plasma membrane, and the phospholipids run to hundreds of chemically distinct species. The diagram above draws one repeating lipid because a diagram has to; treat that as notation.

Numbers help here. There are roughly 5×1065\times10^{6} lipid molecules in a one-micrometre square of bilayer, and about 10910^{9} in the plasma membrane of a small animal cell. A billion components, no bonds between them, and a barrier that has to hold for the four or five days an absorptive cell spends climbing the crypt before it is shed.

That is the problem the rest of the lesson is about.

scenes.title: How far one phospholipid gets in a second
scenes.contentHtml:
How far one phospholipid gets in a second

Fluid is a word that gets attached to membrane diagrams and then does no work. This scene turns it into two numbers and a ratio, because the ratio is where the biology is.

Take one phospholipid in the apical membrane of an absorptive crypt cell. It can do two kinds of moving. It can slide sideways past its neighbours, staying in the layer it is in. Or it can turn over and cross to the other layer, head first through the water-avoiding interior. Both are described as diffusion and the two happen at wildly different rates.

Sideways

A lipid in a bilayer swaps places with a neighbour about 10710^{7} times a second. That gives a lateral diffusion coefficient of roughly 10−8 cm2/s10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm^2/s}.

Convert that into units a cell is measured in. One centimetre is 10410^{4} micrometres, so one square centimetre is 10810^{8} square micrometres, and

For a molecule wandering in a plane, the mean square distance travelled grows in proportion to time:

In words, and this is the reading path if the algebra is not doing anything for you: the square of the typical distance grows in step with the time, so the distance itself grows in step with the square root of the time. Going four times as far takes sixteen times as long.

Worked Example
id worked-example-lipid-crossing-a-cell

Question. A colonic absorptive cell is of order 20 µm across. Taking D=1 μm2s−1D = 1\ \mathrm{\mu m^2\,s^{-1}}, roughly how long does one phospholipid take to diffuse that far in the plane of the membrane?

Step 1. Check the relation on a case you already have. At t=1t = 1 s, ⟨r2⟩=4×1×1=4 μm2\langle r^2 \rangle = 4 \times 1 \times 1 = 4\ \mathrm{\mu m^2}, so r=2r = 2 µm. That is the published figure: an average lipid diffuses about the length of a large bacterium in about a second. The relation reproduces a number nobody fitted it to, which is the cheapest check available and worth doing before trusting it.

Step 2. Rearrange for time. From ⟨r2⟩=4Dt\langle r^2 \rangle = 4Dt, t=r2/(4D)t = r^2 / (4D).

Step 3. Substitute. t=(20 μm)2/(4×1 μm2s−1)=400/4=100t = (20\ \mathrm{\mu m})^2 / (4 \times 1\ \mathrm{\mu m^2\,s^{-1}}) = 400 / 4 = 100 s.

Answer. About a hundred seconds, which is between one and two minutes.

Step 4. Notice the scaling before you leave. Ten times the distance of step 1 cost a hundred times the time. That is the same square-root relation read from the other end: distance grows as the square root of time, so time grows as the square of the distance. It is why diffusion is an excellent way to move a molecule across a cell and a hopeless way to move one across a tissue.

Step 5. Correct the idealisation. The coefficient above comes from a bilayer of pure lipid. In the plasma membrane of a living cell, lipid tracers diffuse about four times more slowly, around 0.5 to 4 µm²/s against 5 to 15 µm²/s in model membranes, because a living membrane is crowded in ways a model bilayer is not. Redo step 3 at D=0.5 μm2s−1D = 0.5\ \mathrm{\mu m^2\,s^{-1}} and you get 200 s. The answer is a couple of minutes either way, and quoting it to three figures would be inventing precision.

Across

Now the other move. A phospholipid crossing from one layer to the other has to drag its water-attracting head through the water-avoiding interior, and that is expensive in exactly the way the first scene described. In synthetic bilayers a given lipid makes that crossing less than once a month. In real plasma membranes, an established difference between the two layers takes several days to run down on its own, without enzymes to help it along.

The ratio is the point

Put the two rates side by side, in the same units.

Movement How often, per lipid Time to move once
Swapping places with a neighbour, in the plane about 10710^{7} per second about 10−710^{-7} s
Turning over to the other layer, in a synthetic bilayer less than about 4×10−74\times10^{-7} per second more than a month
Check
id check-orders-of-magnitude-fluidity

Powers, roots, and scale (PREM-QNT-005) taught you to compare quantities by subtracting their exponents.

Divide the sideways rate by the across rate. How many orders of magnitude separate them? Then say, in one sentence, what that number licenses you to call the membrane.

Dividing 10710^{7} by about 4×10−74\times10^{-7} gives roughly 2.5×10132.5\times10^{13}, so the two rates are separated by about thirteen orders of magnitude. Movement within a layer and movement between layers are not two settings of one dial; they are different physical events with almost nothing in common but the word diffusion.

Thirteen orders of magnitude is what licenses the phrase two-dimensional fluid. A membrane is genuinely liquid in its own plane, so its components mix, rearrange, and find each other freely there. In the third dimension it is effectively solid.

Proteins follow the same rule, which is the strongest evidence that the rule is about the structure and not about lipids. A membrane protein rotates about an axis running across the membrane and many diffuse laterally, and none of them flips over. The classic demonstration fused a mouse cell to a human cell: at first each set of surface proteins stayed on its own half of the joined cell, and within about half an hour the two sets had mixed across the whole surface. Sideways, freely; over, never. A protein inserted the right way round stays that way round for its whole working life, and the fourth scene turns that into an entire layer of biological organisation.

One more thing the ratio buys, and it goes back to scene one. A sheet whose components slide past each other is a sheet that can bend, bud, fuse, close a puncture, and open around a protein being inserted, all without breaking anything. Fluidity is not a decorative property. It is the mechanism behind self-sealing.

scenes.title: Stiffer, looser, and the one that works both ways
scenes.contentHtml:
Stiffer, looser, and the one that works both ways

Fluidity is not one fixed property that membranes either have or lack. It varies with composition and with temperature, it varies between one membrane and another in the same cell, and a cell that loses control of it is a cell in difficulty. This scene names what moves it and in which direction.

A caution about the word first. Fluidity here is a qualitative summary of how easily the hydrocarbon chains move and how loosely they pack. The measurable quantities behind it are viscosity and chain order, and those are what researchers report; no instrument returns a number called fluidity. Treat the word as a direction of travel, which is all this outcome asks you to predict.

Cool a bilayer far enough and it freezes

A bilayer held above a certain temperature is liquid: chains bending, lipids sliding past one another at the rate the previous scene computed. Cool it past that temperature and it changes into a rigid crystalline state, with the chains packed straight and parallel. That change of state is called a phase transition, and the temperature at which it happens depends on what the chains are like.

Two features of the chain set it, and they push the same way.

Chain length. Shorter chains have less surface along which to interact with their neighbours, so they hold together less strongly and the bilayer stays liquid to a lower temperature. Longer chains raise the transition temperature.

Unsaturation. A cis double bond puts a kink in an otherwise straight chain, and kinked chains do not pack tightly against each other. More cis double bonds means a lower transition temperature and a membrane that stays liquid in the cold.

Change Effect on the membrane Mechanism
Longer hydrocarbon chains Less fluid at a given temperature More chain-to-chain interaction along a longer contact
More cis double bonds More fluid at a given temperature Kinks obstruct tight packing
Lower temperature Less fluid, and below the transition the bilayer freezes Less thermal motion in the chains
More cholesterol Two-sided; see below Rigid ring system among flexible chains

Cholesterol does two opposite things and neither is a compromise

Cholesterol is the awkward entry in that table and the one worth getting right, because a learner who memorises a single direction for it will answer half the questions backwards.

Wedged among the hydrocarbon chains, cholesterol's rigid ring system restricts their movement, so a fluid bilayer with cholesterol in it is less fluid than the same bilayer without. That is the first effect and it is the one most people remember.

At the concentrations actually found in eukaryotic plasma membranes, cholesterol also gets in the way of the chains coming together and crystallising. It obstructs the phase transition itself. A membrane loaded with cholesterol is therefore harder to freeze as well as harder to disturb, and across a range of temperatures its behaviour changes less than the same membrane without cholesterol would.

The resolution is that cholesterol is not a fluidity dial with a direction. It is a buffer against change in either direction. Ask what it does and the honest answer is a question back: change relative to what starting state, and at what temperature.

One consequence matters later. Cholesterol makes the bilayer less deformable in the region where it sits, and a less deformable bilayer is less permeable to small water-soluble molecules. Composition therefore sets barrier tightness, before any transport protein is involved at all. Lesson 05 picks that up.

Cells hold their membranes at a working viscosity

Organisms do not let membrane viscosity float with the temperature. They adjust the lipids they build so that viscosity stays roughly where it works, a homeostatic behaviour named homeoviscous adaptation. The adjustments are the ones already in the table: the proportion of chains that disrupt packing, such as unsaturated or branched ones, and the length of the chains.

The clearest demonstration is bacterial. An Escherichia coli strain lacking the enzyme that extends fatty-acid chains grew badly in one growth medium because its membrane fluidity fell, and growth recovered when the missing lipid was supplied. Take that as evidence that the regulation is load-bearing. The study tested no human cell, so it says nothing about one. The ability to adjust membrane composition with temperature is broadly conserved across living things, which is the general statement the evidence supports.

Notice which dial a crypt cell actually holds. It does not set the temperature it works at. What it can change is what it builds its membranes out of, which is why every regulatory mechanism in this area is compositional.

Check
id check-predict-direction

For each change, say whether the membrane becomes more fluid, less fluid, or whether the answer depends on something you should name.

  1. Replacing a saturated tail with one carrying two cis double bonds.
  2. Dropping the temperature by 15 °C.
  3. Doubling the cholesterol content.
  4. Replacing a 16-carbon tail with an 18-carbon tail.

The first makes it more fluid: kinks stop the chains packing. The second makes it less fluid, and if the drop crosses the transition temperature the bilayer freezes instead of merely stiffening. The fourth makes it less fluid: a longer chain interacts with its neighbours along more of its length.

The third is the one that depends. Above the transition temperature more cholesterol restricts chain movement, so the membrane is less fluid. Approaching or below the transition, cholesterol obstructs crystallisation, so the membrane is more fluid than it would otherwise have been. Naming the starting state is part of the answer, and an answer that gives one direction without naming it is incomplete even when the direction happens to be right.

scenes.title: Fluid does not mean shuffled
scenes.contentHtml:
Fluid does not mean shuffled

There is one error that the phrase fluid mosaic invites, and it is worth meeting head on because it wears the look of understanding.

Misconception
id misconception-fluid-implies-uniform

The incorrect model. Everything in a membrane diffuses. Given time, therefore, everything ends up everywhere. A membrane is a well-stirred two-dimensional solution, and any difference between one part of it and another is temporary.

Why it fails. It treats one measured rate as though it were the only one. Movement in the plane is fast, so anything free to move in the plane does mix. Movement between the two layers is slower by about thirteen orders of magnitude, so a difference between the two layers does not run down on any timescale a cell cares about. Diffusion mixes what it can reach, and there is a great deal it cannot reach.

The corrective test. The incorrect model expects a difference between the two layers to even out on the timescale that mixing within a layer takes, which is seconds to minutes. Establish such a difference and measure it. A difference set up in a plasma membrane takes several days to run down without enzymes helping, and in synthetic bilayers a given phospholipid crosses less than once a month. The prediction misses by five or six orders of magnitude, and the model that made it is the one to discard.

The word mosaic never implied a uniform distribution. Evidence for uneven distribution within membranes goes back to the 1960s, before the fluid mosaic model was set out in 1972, and the misreading came later.

Two layers, two compositions

Take the real inventory. In eukaryotic plasma membranes, phosphatidylcholine and the sphingolipids sit mostly in the outer layer, while phosphatidylserine, phosphatidylethanolamine and the phosphoinositides are restricted to the layer facing the cytoplasm.

The diagram in the first scene draws the same lipids on both sides. That is the notation limit mentioned there, and this is where it bites: a membrane's two halves are chemically different, and a picture that draws them the same is leaving out one of the two most important organising facts about the structure.

Slow spontaneous crossing lets a difference persist once it exists. It does not create one. Three families of protein do that work.

  • A flippase moves selected phospholipids, phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine among them, from the outer side to the cytoplasmic side. Flippases belong to the P4-ATPase family and spend ATP.
  • A floppase moves phospholipid in the reverse direction, outward from the cytoplasmic side. Floppases are ABC transporters and also spend ATP.
  • A scramblase moves phospholipids in both directions without specificity and without ATP, randomising the distribution instead of maintaining it.

Read that list as a budget. Maintaining the asymmetry is an ongoing expense, paid continuously, in a structure where the physics is already resisting the change. A cell would not pay it unless the arrangement were doing something.

What the arrangement is for

It is a signal. Phosphatidylserine kept out of the outer layer is a molecule the outside world never sees, so putting it there means something specific.

When a scramblase is switched on and phosphatidylserine appears on the outer surface of an activated platelet, it promotes blood clotting. When it appears on the outer surface of a dying cell, macrophages read it as an instruction to engulf that cell. A crypt cell reaching the top of its climb is a cell about to be removed, and lesson 10 takes up how that removal is controlled.

The general shape of the argument is worth keeping. A cell built a difference that physics tends to preserve, spent energy maintaining it anyway, and then acquired a way to abolish it on demand. The abolition is the message. Nothing about that is available to a well-stirred solution.

Check
id check-asymmetry-mechanism

A drug blocks all flippase activity in a cell without affecting anything else. Predict what happens to the distribution of phosphatidylserine between the two layers over the following minutes, and over the following week. State which rate you used for each answer.

Over minutes, close to nothing. Spontaneous crossing has a half-time of days, so blocking the enzyme that opposes it removes a correction that was operating against a very slow leak. Over a week the asymmetry degrades substantially, because days is now the only timescale in the system. The first answer uses the spontaneous crossing rate; the second uses the same rate run for long enough to matter. Note what the question did not include: a scramblase being switched on would collapse the difference in far less time than either answer, and that is a different mechanism rather than a faster version of this one.

scenes.title: One cell, two membranes, and a fence between them
scenes.contentHtml:
One cell, two membranes, and a fence between them

An absorptive cell in the crypt has a lumen on one side and the rest of the body on the other. Those are different problems, so the cell solves them with different membranes.

A note on where the measurements come from before they are used. Most of the detailed work on brush border lipid composition was done on small-intestinal epithelium, where the microvilli are longest and the tissue purifies cleanly, and some of it in pig. The colonic absorptive cell this block follows carries a shorter version of the same apical specialisation. The argument below is about how a polarised cell organises two membranes, and that argument is not specific to a segment or a species. Where a figure comes from another tissue, the text says so.

The two faces

The apical and basolateral membranes of an intestinal epithelial cell are biochemically and functionally distinct, each with its own set of proteins and its own set of lipids. The apical membrane faces the lumen and does two jobs: it keeps pathogens out, and it processes and takes up nutrients. The basolateral membrane faces the neighbouring cells and the basement membrane, and its business is with them.

The apical membrane is built for a chemically violent neighbourhood

Look at what is on the other side of it. The lumen delivers bile salts, which are detergents, along with the digestive enzymes of the pancreas and bacteria pressed against the surface in enormous numbers. A membrane made to the standard specification would not last there.

The brush border is not made to the standard specification. Its lipid is extraordinarily rich in glycolipids, which exceed 30 per cent of brush border lipid in pig against roughly 5 per cent of total lipid in a typical cell membrane. Glycolipids, cholesterol and sphingomyelin together promote liquid-ordered domains in the outer layer, and in the brush border those domains are thought to be relatively large and stable. That organisation gives the membrane physical and chemical stability against exactly the agents the lumen delivers.

Read that against the previous scene and the picture completes itself. The layer facing the lumen is the layer stiffened by ordered lipid; the layer facing the cytoplasm is the one carrying the signalling lipids. One membrane, two layers, two different jobs, held apart by physics that resists mixing.

The geometry is worth a moment too. A microvillus is about a micrometre long and about a hundred nanometres across, and thousands of them raise the apical surface area of the cell about thirtyfold. The membrane wrapped around one of those cylinders is 5 nanometres thick: twenty times thinner than the cylinder is wide. Lesson 07 takes up what holds a microvillus upright, which is a cytoskeletal question and not a membrane one.

How two fluid membranes stay different

Here is the difficulty. Both membranes are fluid, both are continuous with each other around the top of the cell, and a lipid in the plane crosses a cell in about two minutes. Nothing computed so far explains why the apical composition does not simply flow into the basolateral one.

The answer is a fence, and the experiment that found it is clean enough to reconstruct.

Investigation
id investigation-tight-junction-fence

Setup. Take a polarised epithelial monolayer, in this case a kidney cell line grown as a sheet. Deliver a fluorescent phospholipid specifically into the apical membrane by fusing a liposome with it, then watch whether the label reaches the basolateral surface.

The variable that mattered. Run it twice with liposomes built differently. In the first, the fluorescent lipid sits mostly in the liposome's outer layer, so fusion delivers it to the outer layer of the apical membrane. In the second, the label is in both layers, so fusion delivers it to both layers of the apical membrane.

Result. From the first, the label did not move to the basolateral side. From the second, redistribution to the basolateral membrane happened immediately.

What it shows. The tight junction blocks diffusion of that phospholipid in the outer layer of the plasma membrane and does not block it in the cytoplasmic layer. The barrier is one-sided. That single asymmetry explains how a composition difference survives in a structure whose components are otherwise free to move.

What it does not show. One labelled lipid in one cell line is not every lipid in every epithelium, and a fence that holds the outer layer says nothing about how proteins are delivered to the correct face in the first place. Sorting during delivery is a separate mechanism from retention after arrival.

Protein is held apart the same way. Some plasma-membrane enzymes and transport proteins are confined to the apical surface and others to the basal and lateral surfaces, and that separation of both protein and lipid is attributed at least in part to the tight junction. Lesson 07 is where a junction stops being a line on a diagram and becomes a set of proteins.

The two faces are physically different, and still one membrane

Earlier in this scene the two faces were continuous with each other around the top of the cell, and that has not changed: apical and basolateral are domains of one plasma membrane, not two membranes. What the domains are is physically different, and the strongest single piece of evidence for that is that you can measure the difference.

Solution X-ray scattering across purified membranes from rat liver gives the distance from the phosphate groups on one side to those on the other. Apical plasma membrane came out at 42.5 ± 0.3 Å, basolateral at 35.6 ± 0.6 Å, with the Golgi at 39.5 ± 0.4 Å and the endoplasmic reticulum at 37.5 ± 0.4 Å. The two faces of one polarised cell differ in bilayer thickness by around 7 Å, which is close to 20 per cent. A continuous sheet whose two ends differ by a fifth in thickness is a strong result: it says the difference between the domains is structural and not only a matter of which proteins are parked where.

Two cautions come with that number. It is a hepatocyte measurement, so the apical membrane in question is a bile canalicular one and not an intestinal brush border; the general finding is that a polarised cell's faces are physically different, and the intestinal specifics come from the composition work quoted above. And the phosphate-to-phosphate distance is smaller than the membrane's overall 5-nanometre thickness because it stops at the phosphates instead of at the outer edge of the head groups. When a source gives a number, check where it put the edge.

The same study found that removing cholesterol changed thickness by at most 1 Å, while removing protein changed it by 4 to 5 Å. Membrane protein modulates the thickness of these membranes; cholesterol, at least in this measurement, does not. That is a useful corrective to the previous scene, where cholesterol was doing all the work. Cholesterol governs how the chains move. Protein governs how far apart the two sets of head groups sit.

Where this leaves the block

The membrane is the barrier for everything, and it is organised rather than merely present. Lesson 05 asks how anything crosses it deliberately, and takes sodium-coupled glucose uptake and oral rehydration as its case. Lesson 06 asks how the outside of it carries information inward. Lesson 07 asks what the junction is actually made of. Every one of those questions assumes what this lesson established: two molecules of lipid, fluid in the plane, effectively solid across it, and sorted.

scenes.title: Practice: predict the direction, then defend it
scenes.contentHtml:
Practice: predict the direction, then defend it

Three passes. The first hands you the relation, the second hands you less, and the third hands you a situation and nothing else.

Pass one, with the reasoning named for you

Check
id check-practice-composition-prediction

Two related organisms live at different temperatures, one at about 5 °C and one at about 35 °C. Both hold their membranes at a working viscosity.

  1. Which one would you expect to build more cis double bonds into its membrane lipids, and why?
  2. Which one would you expect to build longer hydrocarbon chains, and why?
  3. Name one thing you would have to measure to find out whether your prediction is right, and one reason it might fail.

The cold organism needs more cis double bonds. Kinks obstruct packing, so a kinked membrane stays liquid at a lower temperature, and an organism at 5 °C is closer to freezing its membranes than one at 35 °C. The warm organism can afford longer chains: longer chains interact more strongly along their length and raise the transition temperature, which is a problem in the cold and not in the warmth. Both answers come out of the same two rows of the third scene's table.

To test it you would measure the fatty-acid composition of membrane lipid from each organism grown at its own temperature, and compare chain lengths and the proportion of unsaturated chains. It might fail because the general principle names several strategies, including branched chains and changes to the head groups, and an organism may reach the same viscosity by a route other than the two you predicted. A prediction about the outcome is safer than a prediction about the mechanism.

Pass two, with the numbers and not the method

Check
id check-practice-diffusion-ladder

Take D=1 μm2s−1D = 1\ \mathrm{\mu m^2\,s^{-1}} for a lipid in the plane of a membrane, and ⟨r2⟩=4Dt\langle r^2 \rangle = 4Dt.

  1. A microvillus is about 1 µm long. How long does a lipid take to diffuse from its base to its tip?
  2. The cell is about 20 µm across. How long to cross that?
  3. Question 2 is twenty times the distance of question 1. By what factor is it longer in time, and why is that not twenty?
  4. A lipid is delivered into the outer layer of the apical membrane. With no enzyme acting on it, roughly how long before it appears in the inner layer, and what would change that answer to seconds?

For the microvillus, t=r2/(4D)=1/4=0.25t = r^2/(4D) = 1/4 = 0.25 s. For the cell width, t=400/4=100t = 400/4 = 100 s. That is four hundred times longer for twenty times the distance, because the relation puts time in proportion to the square of the distance, and 202=40020^2 = 400. A learner who answers twenty has used a proportional model where a square-law model belongs, which is the single most common way this arithmetic goes wrong.

For the fourth part, days. Spontaneous crossing between the layers has a half-time of several days, so on its own the lipid stays where it was put for a very long time by cellular standards. A scramblase switched on in that membrane would move phospholipids in both directions without ATP and randomise the distribution, collapsing the difference in seconds to minutes. Note that the enzyme changes the mechanism rather than accelerating the spontaneous one.

Pass three, with nothing but the situation

Check
id check-practice-fence-failure

A cultured epithelial monolayer is treated so that its tight junctions come apart, leaving the cells alive, still attached to each other by other junctions, and with normal membranes.

  1. Predict what happens over the next few minutes to a fluorescent lipid sitting in the outer layer of the apical membrane.
  2. Predict what happens to a fluorescent lipid sitting in the inner layer of the same membrane.
  3. A colleague concludes that the tight junction is therefore what puts each membrane protein on the correct face in the first place. Say what is wrong with that inference and what evidence would settle it.
  4. State one thing about the apical membrane that this treatment would not change.

The outer-layer label spreads to the basolateral surface. It was the fence that was holding it, and lateral diffusion crosses a cell in a couple of minutes once nothing is in the way. The inner-layer label does essentially nothing new: the fence never acted on the inner layer, so that label was already free to redistribute and had done so.

The colleague's inference confuses two mechanisms. The fence experiment shows the junction retains an outer-layer difference that already exists; it says nothing about how a protein reaches the apical face to begin with. Sorting during delivery and retention after arrival are separate processes, and the treatment described tests only the second. Settling it needs an experiment that follows newly made protein from synthesis to surface and asks where it is first inserted, with the junction intact and again with it disrupted.

The thing that would not change is the apical membrane's own lipid composition, at least at first. Its glycolipid enrichment and the liquid-ordered domains those lipids form are properties of what the membrane is made of, and a junction coming apart does not remove a glycolipid from a bilayer. Composition and confinement are two different mechanisms holding the same arrangement in place, which is why the cell uses both.

Accessibility and alternatives

Every figure in this lesson carries a long description that states its content and the conclusion drawn from it, and no task depends on seeing either one. The membrane components figure is an inventory of parts, all of which are also named and defined in the prose of the first scene. The two-faces diagram is a set of labelled relationships, all of which are stated in the fifth scene's sentences.

Both figures use colour, and neither carries information by colour alone: every element the lesson refers to is labelled in text.

The two displayed relations in the second scene are each restated in words next to the symbols. The unit conversion is written out in full, and the square-root behaviour of diffusion distance is given as a sentence beside the equation, so the relation can be followed without reading the algebra. The tables are semantic text and read correctly in a screen reader in row order, and every direction they record is also given in the surrounding prose.

No task in this lesson requires personal physiology, health data, laboratory access, or physical practical work.

Recovery route

If the practice went badly, the useful question is which of four things broke.

A direction came out backwards. Go back to the table in the third scene and re-read the mechanism column instead of the direction column. Every direction in this lesson follows from one of two mechanisms: how easily the chains pack, and how much thermal motion they have. A direction memorised without its mechanism will invert under a rephrased question.

Cholesterol went one way when it should have gone both. Reread the second half of the third scene. The test is whether you asked relative to what starting state. If your answer did not name a temperature or a starting fluidity, it was incomplete regardless of which direction you chose.

The diffusion arithmetic gave a factor of twenty instead of four hundred. Reread the fourth step of the worked example in the second scene, then redo pass two. Proportional models (PREM-QNT-010) is where the difference between a proportional and a square-law relation was set out, and this is the same distinction in a new place.

The fence and the sorting got mixed up. Reread the investigation in the fifth scene, paying attention to what the experiment varied and what it left alone. The experiment moved a label into one layer or two and watched where it went. Nothing in it followed a newly made molecule from synthesis to surface, so nothing in it can answer a question about delivery.

If more than one of those applies, work through the second and third scenes again before the fourth and fifth. Scenes four and five are both built on the rate comparison, and they do not stand up on their own if that comparison is unclear.

scenes.title: Clinical wrap-up: a drug that can only tell two membranes apart by their sterol
scenes.contentHtml:
Clinical wrap-up: a drug that can only tell two membranes apart by their sterol

Callout
id callout-teaching-boundary

Teaching example, not medical advice. Nothing here is a dose, an indication, a contraindication, a monitoring plan, or a recommendation about any patient. No dose, threshold, regimen, or duration appears anywhere in this lesson. This is a reasoning exercise about membrane composition, worked with the tools the lesson has already built.

The target of amphotericin B is a lipid, and it is the lipid the third scene spent half its length on.

Fungi build their membranes with ergosterol where human cells build theirs with cholesterol. Both are sterols, both sit among the hydrocarbon chains, and both do the same structural job. They are not the same molecule, and the difference is enough to hang a drug on.

Step one: what is the target

Amphotericin B interacts with ergosterol rather than with an enzyme. Two accounts of what follows are current. In one, the drug and the sterol together form pores through which ions leak. In the other, the drug assembles into large aggregates sitting outside the membrane and pulls ergosterol out of the bilayer into them, which is described as a sterol sponge. The disagreement is not only about the route. In the pore account the drug and the sterol build an ion-conducting structure together and the sterol stays in the membrane as part of it; in the sponge account the sterol leaves. Only the second ends in a membrane that no longer has the sterol it was built around.

Take the sponge account for a moment, because it is the one this lesson's model speaks to. A membrane stripped of its sterol has lost the component that restricts chain movement, obstructs the phase transition, and holds down permeability to small water-soluble molecules. Those consequences are consequences of membrane behaviour, and you can predict their direction from the third scene without knowing anything else about fungal biology.

The pore account arrives at leakage by a different road: the structure the drug and the sterol form is itself the hole. Both accounts predict a membrane that leaks, which is why the disagreement has been hard to settle from the outcome alone. They do not predict the same membrane. Keep the two apart when you reason forward from either, because a prediction that starts from sterol removal is a prediction about only one of them.

Step two: why it is more toxic to a fungus than to us

Two reasons, and they are different in kind.

The first is chemical. Three interactions bind the drug to ergosterol: van der Waals forces, a network of hydrogen bonds, and an electronic interaction between the ergosterol side chain and the drug's polyene tail. That third attachment point does not form when the drug binds cholesterol.

The second is compositional. Fungal membranes carry a higher ratio of ergosterol to phospholipid than mammalian membranes carry of cholesterol to phospholipid. Even a drug with no chemical preference would find more target per unit area in the fungus.

Check
id check-selectivity-is-a-ratio

The drug's affinity for ergosterol is about ten times its affinity for cholesterol.

  1. Does a tenfold preference mean human membranes are unaffected? Answer before reading on, and say what a tenfold preference does mean.
  2. Human cells are exposed to this drug. Predict, from the third scene alone, one direction in which their membrane behaviour changes.
  3. What would have to be true of a sterol for a drug like this to be entirely selective?

A tenfold preference means the drug binds ergosterol about ten times more readily. It does not mean it leaves cholesterol alone, and non-selective disruption of mammalian cell membranes does occur. A ratio is not a switch, and reading a selectivity figure as though it were one is the single most common error in thinking about drug toxicity.

For the second part: removing cholesterol from a membrane removes what was holding down permeability to small water-soluble molecules, so that membrane leaks more than it did. Predicting the direction is available to you; predicting which tissue suffers most is not, and that is a question about exposure, which this lesson does not cover.

For the third part, the drug would need a binding requirement that the human sterol cannot satisfy at all, rather than one it satisfies less well. The electronic interaction with the ergosterol side chain is close to that: it is described as absent with cholesterol. What stops the drug being entirely selective is that the other two interactions are not.

Step three: where the toxicity lands, and why formulation helps

The kidney takes the worst of it. Two contributions are described: the drug constricts the afferent arterioles that feed the filtering units, which lowers renal blood flow and filtration; and cells take the drug up through low-density-lipoprotein receptors, which raises how much of it they see. Separately, mononuclear immune cells recognise the drug through two surface receptors, which is the route to the reactions that can accompany an infusion.

Notice that only the first of those is a membrane-composition story. The second is a delivery story, and it is why formulation changes the picture. Preparations in which the drug is associated with lipid show less kidney toxicity than the older deoxycholate preparation, and the liposomal one also produces fewer infusion reactions. Nothing about the drug's affinity for either sterol has changed. What changed is where the drug goes and what it is presented in.

That distinction between what a molecule binds and where a molecule ends up is worth carrying forward. This lesson can predict the first and cannot predict the second.

Step four: resistance, which turns the same dial

The commonest way a fungus escapes this drug is by altering the sterol composition of its own membrane. Loss of function in the genes of the ergosterol pathway, ERG11 and ERG3 among them, replaces ergosterol with other sterols: lanosterol, eburicol, 4,14-dimethyl-zymosterol.

The fungus is doing exactly what the third scene described a cell doing, and for a different reason. Composition is the adjustable part of a membrane, so composition is what changes under selection, and a drug that targets a compositional feature is a drug whose target can be composed differently.

This is where the lesson leaves you with a question instead of an answer. Sterols are not interchangeable structurally; ergosterol and lanosterol are different molecules and this lesson has given you every reason to expect them to behave differently among the hydrocarbon chains. Whether a resistant strain pays for its substitution in altered membrane behaviour is a real research question and the review cited here does not answer it. Being able to formulate that question precisely, from a sterol swap to a prediction about chain packing, is what the last five scenes were for.

assessment.title: Membrane structure and fluidity mastery check

items.prompt: A cell line is grown at 37 degrees Celsius and then moved to 25 degrees Celsius, where it is kept for several generations. For each of the following, state the direction of the change and the mechanism behind it in one sentence: (a) what happens to membrane fluidity in the minutes immediately after the temperature drop, before the cell has changed anything; (b) what change to the proportion of cis-unsaturated chains you would expect the cell to make over the following generations, and why; (c) what change to hydrocarbon chain length you would expect, and why; (d) name one reason your predictions in (b) and (c) could both be wrong while the cell still ends up with a membrane at a working viscosity.

answer.correct: (a) Fluidity falls immediately. Less thermal energy means less chain motion and tighter packing, and if the drop crossed the phase transition the bilayer would move towards the rigid crystalline state rather than merely stiffening. (b) The cell should raise the proportion of cis-unsaturated chains. A cis double bond kinks a chain so the chains pack together less easily, which lowers the phase transition temperature and keeps the membrane liquid in the cold. (c) The cell should shorten its chains. A shorter chain has less length along which to interact with its neighbours, so shorter chains also lower the transition temperature. (d) The general principle names more than two levers. An organism can hold viscosity steady by changing branched-chain content or by changing the lipid head groups instead, so a correct prediction about the outcome, a membrane held at working viscosity, is compatible with a wrong prediction about which mechanism was used. The evidence for the mechanisms is also largely bacterial, so a mammalian cell line need not use the same route.
answer.summary: Fluidity falls at once; the cell should then raise cis-unsaturation and shorten chains, both of which lower the transition temperature; and the prediction can fail on mechanism because branched chains and head groups are alternative routes to the same viscosity.
answer.reasoning: Award one point for (a) only when the answer gives both the direction and a thermal-motion or packing mechanism; naming the phase transition is credited but not required. Award one point for (b) only when the direction is upward and the reason is the kink obstructing packing, rather than an unexplained association between unsaturation and fluidity. Award one point for (c) only when the direction is towards shorter chains and the reason is reduced chain-to-chain interaction along a shorter contact. Award one point for (d) only when the answer identifies an alternative compositional route, such as branched chains or head groups, or the bacterial provenance of the evidence, and connects it to the difference between predicting an outcome and predicting a mechanism. An answer that says only 'biology is complicated' does not earn this point.
acceptableResponses: For (a), 'less fluid, less thermal motion so the chains pack more tightly' is sufficient.
For (d), either the alternative-mechanism route or the bacterial-provenance limitation earns the point; naming both is not required.
Answers that use 'more ordered' or 'more viscous' in place of 'less fluid' are equivalent and acceptable.
commonErrors: Giving (b) and (c) as memorised associations with no mechanism, which does not survive a rephrased question.
Predicting longer chains in the cold by reasoning that longer chains are somehow more flexible; chain length raises the transition temperature.
Treating (a) as a question about what the cell does, when it asks what happens before the cell does anything.
Answering (d) with a generic hedge instead of naming an alternative route or the limits of the evidence.

items.prompt: A bilayer built from saturated chains is held at a temperature just below its phase transition, so the chains have packed into the rigid crystalline state. Cholesterol is then added until it makes up a large fraction of the lipid. What happens, and why?

options.text: More fluid than the same bilayer without cholesterol, because cholesterol prevents the hydrocarbon chains from coming together and crystallising.
Less fluid, because cholesterol's rigid ring system restricts the movement of the hydrocarbon chains.
No change, because cholesterol sits at the boundary between the two leaflets and does not interact with the hydrocarbon chains.
More fluid, because cholesterol introduces cis double bonds into the neighbouring hydrocarbon chains.
Less fluid, because cholesterol increases bilayer thickness and a thicker bilayer is always more ordered.

answer.summary: Below the phase transition, cholesterol obstructs crystallisation, so the membrane is more fluid than the same bilayer without it.
answer.reasoning: Cholesterol acts in two opposite directions depending on the starting state. Above the phase transition, its rigid rings restrict chain movement and the membrane becomes less fluid, which is the second option and is the right mechanism attached to the wrong starting state. Below the transition, the chains are trying to crystallise and cholesterol gets in the way of that, so the membrane stays more fluid than it otherwise would. The question specifies a temperature below the transition, so the second effect is the one operating. The third option is false, since cholesterol is wedged among the chains. The fourth is false, since cholesterol does not modify neighbouring chains chemically. The fifth attaches a real thickness effect to an invented rule; the study that measured bilayer thickness across compartments found cholesterol depletion changed thickness by at most one angstrom, with protein doing the modulating.
commonErrors: Choosing the second option, which is the commonest error and reflects a single memorised direction for cholesterol rather than a dependence on the starting state.
Choosing any option without noticing that the prompt fixed the temperature below the transition, which is the whole content of the question.

items.prompt: Take a lateral diffusion coefficient of D = 2 micrometres squared per second and the two-dimensional relation mean square displacement equals 4Dt. (a) How long does a lipid take to diffuse 4 micrometres in the plane of the membrane? Show the arithmetic and carry the units. (b) How long to diffuse 40 micrometres, and by what factor is that longer than your answer to (a)? (c) A lipid delivered into the outer leaflet of that same membrane is still, days later, mostly in the outer leaflet. Explain why that is consistent with your answers and not in tension with them. (d) The coefficient you were given, 2 micrometres squared per second, is itself in the range measured in living cell membranes. Given that, say whether protein crowding is a further reason your answer to (a) is too short, and name one thing about a real polarised cell that this relation does not represent at all.

answer.correct: (a) t = r squared divided by 4D = (4 micrometres) squared / (4 x 2 micrometres squared per second) = 16 / 8 = 2 seconds. (b) t = (40) squared / 8 = 1600 / 8 = 200 seconds, which is 100 times longer than 2 seconds. Ten times the distance costs a hundred times the time because the relation puts time in proportion to the square of the distance. (c) The two are different movements. The arithmetic describes lateral diffusion within one leaflet, which is fast. Crossing to the other leaflet means dragging a water-attracting head group through the water-avoiding interior, which is rare: less than once a month per molecule in synthetic bilayers, and days of half-time for an established asymmetry in a plasma membrane. A membrane is fluid within its plane and effectively solid across it, so both observations describe the same structure. (d) No. Crowding is already inside the number. Lipid tracers in a living cell membrane diffuse about four times more slowly than in a model membrane, roughly 0.5 to 4 micrometres squared per second against 5 to 15, because proteins, ordered domains and the cytoskeleton obstruct the path, and the 2 given here sits inside that measured range. Applying the slowdown again would count it twice. What the relation does not represent is whether the journey is available at all: in a polarised cell the tight junction is a fence in the outer leaflet, so a lipid delivered into the outer leaflet of the apical membrane does not reach the basolateral face however long it diffuses. The relation gives the time for unobstructed diffusion over a distance. Whether the path exists is a separate question, and no value of D answers it.
answer.summary: 2 seconds; 200 seconds, a factor of 100 for ten times the distance; the leaflet observation concerns a different movement that is slower by many orders of magnitude; and the crowding correction is already inside the given coefficient, while what the relation omits is whether the path exists at all.
answer.reasoning: Award one point for (a) only when the rearrangement to t = r squared over 4D is used with units carried and the answer is 2 seconds. Award one point for (b) only when the answer is 200 seconds and the factor is identified as 100 with the square-law reason given; a factor of 10 shows a proportional model used where a square-law model belongs and does not earn the point. Award one point for (c) and (d) together, and only when (c) distinguishes lateral diffusion from transbilayer crossing rather than describing the leaflet result as slow diffusion, and (d) recognises that the given coefficient is already a living-cell value, so crowding is not a further correction, and names something the relation does not represent, the tight-junction fence being the one this lesson supplies. An answer that applies the crowding slowdown on top of the given D has double-counted it and does not earn the point, even though the physics it cites is real.
acceptableResponses: Any correct algebraic route to 2 seconds and 200 seconds is acceptable.

For (d), any obstruction the relation does not contain is acceptable in place of the fence, including confinement to an ordered domain or corralling by the cytoskeleton, provided the answer treats it as a limit on the model rather than as a further multiplier on the given coefficient.

For (c), an answer framed as 'the membrane is a two-dimensional fluid, so the third dimension is a different problem' earns the point when it also names the head group and the water-avoiding interior.

For (d), noting that displacement over tens of micrometres departs from the square-law relation because diffusion at that scale is not free is a stronger answer than the expected one and earns the point.
commonErrors: Reporting the factor in (b) as 10 rather than 100.
Forgetting the factor of 4 and computing t = r squared over D.
Treating (c) as evidence that the membrane is not really fluid, rather than as evidence that fluidity is directional.
Answering (d) by applying the living-cell slowdown to a coefficient that was already measured in a living cell, which counts the same obstruction twice.
Answering (d) with a change that would shorten the time, such as a higher temperature, which does not address what was asked.

items.prompt: An absorptive intestinal cell keeps two separations going at once: a difference between the two leaflets of one membrane, and a difference between its apical and basolateral membranes. For each separation, name the mechanism that holds it and one observation that demonstrates that mechanism is doing the work. Then consider interrupting the cell's ATP supply for several hours as a way of telling the two mechanisms apart, and say what that experiment would and would not establish.

answer.correct: The leaflet difference is created and maintained by ATP-driven transporters, principally flippases moving phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine to the cytoplasmic leaflet, and it persists because spontaneous crossing between leaflets is very slow. The demonstrating observations are that flippases are ATP-dependent and that, once established, an asymmetry takes a half-time of several days to run down without enzymatic help. The apical-to-basolateral difference is held by the tight junction acting as a fence. The demonstrating observation is the liposome-fusion experiment in a polarised kidney monolayer: a fluorescent phospholipid delivered into the outer leaflet of the apical membrane did not reach the basolateral side, while the same marker delivered into both leaflets redistributed immediately, showing that the fence operates in the outer leaflet and not the cytoplasmic one. Composition contributes too, since the apical membrane's glycolipid enrichment and ordered domains are properties of what it is made of. Interrupting ATP for several hours establishes less than it looks like it should, because it is not a selective intervention. One half of the reasoning does hold. If the flippases alone stopped, the leaflet difference would lose little over several hours, because what preserves it is the slowness of spontaneous crossing rather than the pumps: an established asymmetry runs down with a half-time of days. That is the real lesson, and it is about timescale, not about one separation being ATP-dependent and the other not. The other half does not hold. Removing ATP removes it from everything, including the cytoskeleton the junction is anchored to and the transport and calcium handling the junction depends on, so the fence cannot be assumed to sit there intact while only the flippases stop. This lesson's sources establish that spontaneous flip-flop is slow and that the junction is a fence in the outer leaflet. They do not establish what a general energy failure does to that fence, and it is not safe to assume nothing. So the experiment cannot attribute what survives to the mechanism being asked about: an intervention that hits everything cannot isolate one thing. Separating a pump from a barrier needs an intervention aimed at one of them.
answer.summary: Leaflet difference: ATP-driven flippases create it and slow spontaneous flip-flop preserves it, evidenced by ATP dependence and a days-long decay half-time. Apical against basolateral: the tight-junction fence, evidenced by the outer-leaflet-only liposome result, with composition contributing. A general ATP interruption cannot tell the two apart, because it removes energy from the junction's own supporting structures as well as from the pumps; what it does show is that the leaflet difference is stable on the wrong timescale to be pump-maintained hour to hour.
answer.reasoning: Award one point for naming ATP-driven flippases as the maintaining mechanism for the leaflet difference together with slow spontaneous flip-flop as the reason it persists. Award one point for the demonstrating observation for that separation, either the ATP dependence of the transporters or the days-long decay half-time. Award one point for naming the tight junction as a fence and reconstructing the liposome experiment, including the contrast between outer-leaflet and both-leaflet delivery; an answer that names the junction without an observation does not earn this point. Award one point for the ATP-interruption reasoning when it does both of two things: identifies that several hours is short against a days-long decay, so stopping the pumps alone would remove little of the leaflet asymmetry, and recognises that removing ATP is not selective, so what happens to the junction is not something the intervention or this lesson's sources settle. An answer that asserts the leaflet difference collapses within hours has confused maintenance with the barrier that makes maintenance cheap. An answer that confidently reports both separations surviving intact has treated a global intervention as a targeted one, and earns the point only if it names that as an assumption.
acceptableResponses: Mentioning scramblase activation as a faster route to collapsing the leaflet difference is correct and does not lose a point, provided the answer notes that this is a different mechanism rather than the ATP interruption described.
Crediting composition, in the form of glycolipid enrichment and ordered domains, alongside the junction for the apical-to-basolateral separation is correct and welcome.
An answer that says the leaflet asymmetry degrades over days and is therefore only partly reduced after several hours is equivalent to 'largely survives' for the first half of the reasoning.
Proposing a better-aimed experiment, such as inhibiting or deleting a single flippase rather than starving the whole cell, is a stronger answer than the expected one and earns the point.
commonErrors: Claiming the tight junction blocks both leaflets, which the experiment specifically rules out.
Claiming the tight junction is what puts each protein on the correct face, which confuses retention with sorting.
Asserting that stopping ATP collapses lipid asymmetry within hours, which ignores the rate that made the asymmetry stable in the first place.
Treating ATP starvation as though it stopped only the flippases, which is the assumption the last part of this item is asking you to notice.
Naming mechanisms without any observation, which answers a different question from the one asked.

items.prompt: A research group describes an experimental antifungal that removes ergosterol from fungal membranes and reports that it binds ergosterol about thirty times more readily than it binds cholesterol. Using only the membrane reasoning from this lesson, answer four things. (a) Predict two directions in which a fungal membrane's behaviour changes once its sterol is removed. (b) Say what a thirtyfold binding preference does and does not tell you about effects on human cells. (c) A colleague proposes that raising the dose until fungal killing is complete is safe because the preference is so large. Say what is wrong with that reasoning in terms of membranes rather than in terms of clinical practice. (d) Predict one route by which a fungal population could become resistant, and state what you would measure to see whether that route carried a cost. This is a teaching exercise; do not give clinical advice, doses, or recommendations.

answer.correct: (a) A sterol-depleted membrane loses what was restricting chain movement and obstructing crystallisation, so its fluidity becomes more sensitive to temperature and to composition than it was; and it loses the reduction in deformability that sterol provided, so it becomes more permeable to small water-soluble molecules. Either direction, expressed as loss of the buffering role or as increased leakiness, is the point. (b) A thirtyfold preference says the drug binds one sterol about thirty times more readily than the other. It does not say human membranes are untouched, because a preference is a ratio and not a switch; a drug with a tenfold preference is already known to disrupt mammalian membranes non-selectively. (c) Raising the dose raises the occupancy of both sterols together, and the margin does not hold while it does. Binding saturates. The preferred target fills up first, so as the dose climbs the fungal sterol approaches full occupancy while the human sterol keeps rising, and the gap between them closes: the thirtyfold advantage is largest at low occupancy and worth nothing once both are saturated. Raising the dose until fungal killing is complete is deliberately driving the system towards the end where the preference has been spent. There is a second problem with the reasoning even before that. A binding preference is a ratio of affinities, and an affinity ratio is not an effect ratio; getting from one to the other needs how much drug reaches each membrane, how much sterol is there to bind, how many bound molecules it takes to do anything, and how each membrane responds. The colleague has treated a ratio as a threshold, and assumed the ratio survives the dose increase. Neither holds. (d) The fungus could alter its own membrane sterol, replacing ergosterol with another sterol the drug binds poorly, which is the known route for this drug class. To see whether that carried a cost I would measure the membrane behaviour the substituted sterol is now responsible for: chain order or viscosity across a range of temperatures, and passive permeability to a small water-soluble tracer, comparing resistant and parent strains.
answer.summary: Loss of sterol removes both the buffering of fluidity and the reduction in permeability; a thirtyfold preference is a ratio rather than a switch, and because binding saturates the preferred target fills first, so raising the dose narrows the margin rather than preserving it; resistance most plausibly comes from substituting the sterol, and the cost would show up in chain order or viscosity across temperature and in passive permeability.
answer.reasoning: Award one point for (a) only when two directions are given and each is tied to a stated property of sterol in a membrane; two restatements of the same effect earn one direction, not two. Award one point for (b) only when the answer identifies the preference as a ratio rather than an absence of effect. Award one point for (c) only when the argument is made in membrane terms and gets the direction right: raising the dose raises occupancy of both sterols, and because binding saturates the preferred one fills first, so the margin narrows as the dose climbs. An answer stating that the ratio stays fixed while the absolute effect rises has the second half right and the first half wrong, and does not earn the point, because a fixed ratio is the reassuring version of the error the item is built around. Recognising instead that an affinity ratio is not an effect ratio without exposure, sterol abundance, stoichiometry and response also earns the point. An answer that appeals to clinical practice or to toxicity generally, without a membrane-level argument, does not. Award one point for (d) only when the resistance route is a change in the membrane's own sterol composition and the proposed measurement is a membrane behaviour rather than a growth or survival readout alone. An answer containing a dose, an indication, or a clinical recommendation loses that point regardless of its other content, because the prompt set that boundary.
acceptableResponses: For (a), 'the membrane is less able to hold its properties steady as temperature changes' and 'the membrane leaks small water-soluble molecules more readily' are the two expected directions; equivalent phrasings are acceptable.
For (d), naming a specific biosynthetic step is not required; 'replaces ergosterol with a sterol the drug binds poorly' is sufficient.
Proposing an additional measurement, such as sensitivity to a membrane-disrupting agent, alongside the two named is acceptable.

For (c), either route earns the point: that saturation narrows the margin as the dose rises, or that an affinity ratio cannot be converted into an effect ratio from affinity alone. Both together is a full answer and is what a strong response looks like.
commonErrors: Answering (b) by restating the preference as evidence of safety, which is the error the item is built around.
Answering (c) with the claim that the ratio between the two effects holds steady as the dose rises, which sounds like the careful answer and is the opposite of what saturable binding does.
Answering (c) with clinical reasoning about monitoring or dosing, which the prompt excludes and which the lesson never taught.
Predicting in (a) that the membrane becomes less permeable, which reverses the direction sterol acts in.
Proposing in (d) a resistance route that changes the drug rather than the membrane, which the question's framing about membranes does not support.
