claims.scope: Eukaryotic plasma membranes. Used to show that a diagram drawing one repeating lipid is notation rather than composition.
claims.uncertainty: The sterol share is an upper figure across membranes and cell types rather than a value for any particular membrane; organelle membranes carry much less.

claims.statement: There are approximately 5 x 10^6 lipid molecules in a one-micrometre square of lipid bilayer, and about 10^9 lipid molecules in the plasma membrane of a small animal cell.
claims.scope: Order-of-magnitude counts for a lipid bilayer and for a small animal cell's plasma membrane, used to convey how many unbonded components a membrane holds together.
claims.uncertainty: Both figures are approximations that depend on lipid packing density and on assumed cell size.

claims.statement: A colonic crypt is an invagination of the epithelial lining whose base holds the stem-cell niche; cells differentiate as they migrate upward and are fully differentiated at the crypt top, absorptive cells are replaced every four to five days within a lining that renews every three to five days, and the colonocytes maintain the integrity of the epithelial barrier.
claims.scope: Human colonic crypt. Carried forward from PREM-BIO-001 so that this lesson's membrane material stays attached to the block's running case.
claims.uncertainty: The renewal figures are population-level intervals rather than a claim that every crypt cell shares one lifetime, as PREM-BIO-001 also records.

claims.statement: A lipid molecule in a bilayer exchanges places with its neighbours within a monolayer about 10^7 times per second, giving a lateral diffusion coefficient of about 10^-8 cm2 per second, so that an average lipid molecule diffuses about 2 micrometres in about one second.
claims.scope: Lipid bilayers, with the quoted coefficient characteristic of a fluid bilayer rather than of any particular cell membrane.
claims.uncertainty: The coefficient is an order of magnitude. Measured values depend on lipid composition, temperature, and technique, and the lesson immediately gives the lower range measured in living cells.

claims.statement: Lipid tracers diffuse on average about four times faster in model membranes than in the plasma membrane of living cells, with reported values around 5 to 15 micrometres squared per second in fluid model membranes against 0.5 to 4 micrometres squared per second in cell membranes.
claims.scope: Comparison of tracer diffusion in fluid model membranes with living-cell plasma membranes, used to correct the idealisation in the lesson's worked example.
claims.uncertainty: Reported diffusion coefficients depend heavily on tracer, technique, and observation timescale, and the review cited makes that variability one of its central points.

claims.statement: Movement of a phospholipid from one leaflet to the other is rare: in synthetic bilayers a given molecule flip-flops less than once a month, and once asymmetry is established in a plasma membrane, disrupting it without enzymatic help has a half-time of several days.
claims.scope: Spontaneous, unassisted transbilayer movement of phospholipids. The two figures come from different systems, a synthetic bilayer and a plasma membrane, and the lesson attributes each to its own system.
claims.uncertainty: Rates vary by lipid class; cholesterol, for instance, crosses far more readily than a phospholipid. Neither figure describes protein-mediated movement, which is the subject of a separate claim.

claims.statement: The lipid bilayer behaves as a two-dimensional fluid: its components diffuse readily within the plane of each layer while movement between layers is comparatively negligible.
claims.scope: Lipid bilayers above their phase transition, which covers biological membranes at working temperature.
claims.uncertainty: The description is a model with limits the lesson states: real cell membranes contain domains, protein obstacles and cytoskeletal constraints that make diffusion slower and less uniform than in an ideal plane.

claims.statement: A bilayer stays fluid to a lower temperature when its hydrocarbon chains are short or carry double bonds: a shorter chain interacts less with its neighbours, and a cis double bond kinks the chain so the chains pack together less easily.
claims.scope: Lipid bilayers generally. Stated as directions of effect rather than as quantified shifts in transition temperature.
claims.uncertainty: Real membranes mix many lipid species, so the composite behaviour is not a simple sum of single-species transition temperatures.

claims.statement: A lipid bilayer changes from a liquid state to a rigid crystalline state below a characteristic temperature, a change of state called a phase transition.
claims.scope: Lipid bilayers. The lesson uses the transition to explain why temperature and composition act on the same property.
claims.uncertainty: In a membrane of mixed composition the transition is broad rather than sharp, and cholesterol obstructs it further, which the lesson states in the same scene.

claims.statement: Cholesterol tends to make lipid bilayers less fluid, and at the high concentrations found in most eukaryotic plasma membranes it also prevents the hydrocarbon chains from coming together and crystallising, so it inhibits possible phase transitions.
claims.scope: Eukaryotic plasma membranes at physiological cholesterol content. The lesson presents the effect as buffering against change in either direction rather than as a single direction.
claims.uncertainty: Which effect dominates depends on the starting state and the temperature, which is exactly the point the lesson makes; a single-direction answer is incomplete rather than simply wrong.

claims.statement: Cholesterol makes the lipid bilayer less deformable in the region where it sits and thereby decreases the permeability of the bilayer to small water-soluble molecules.
claims.scope: Cholesterol-containing lipid bilayers. Used to show that composition sets barrier tightness before any transport protein is involved, and to let the learner predict the direction of change when a drug removes sterol from a membrane.
claims.uncertainty: A directional statement about passive permeability to small water-soluble molecules; it does not quantify permeability and says nothing about protein-mediated transport, which lesson 05 owns.

claims.statement: Homeoviscous adaptation holds cell membranes at a fixed viscosity across growth temperatures by varying the proportion of packing-disrupting lipids such as unsaturated or branched-chain fatty acids and by varying acyl chain length; the trait is broadly conserved, and an Escherichia coli strain deleted for fabF grew severely poorly in succinate medium through decreased membrane fluidity, recovering when the missing lipid was supplied.
claims.scope: The definition and the compositional strategies are general and the source describes broad conservation across prokaryotes, eukaryotic microorganisms and multicellular organisms. The growth-defect experiment is bacterial and is presented as bacterial in the lesson.
claims.uncertainty: No human or mammalian cell was tested in the cited study. The lesson therefore uses the bacterial result as evidence that the regulation is load-bearing and does not assert a corresponding human phenotype.

claims.statement: The two leaflets of a eukaryotic plasma membrane hold different lipids: phosphatidylcholine and the sphingolipids sit primarily in the outer leaflet, while phosphatidylserine, phosphatidylethanolamine and the phosphoinositides are restricted to the cytoplasmic leaflet.
claims.scope: Eukaryotic plasma membranes. Three independent sources give the same distribution, which is why the lesson treats it as established rather than as a single report.
claims.uncertainty: Asymmetry is a strong preference rather than an absolute partition, and it is actively maintained, so it can be regulated away as the lesson goes on to describe.

claims.statement: Lipid asymmetry is maintained and abolished by three transporter families: flippases, which are P4-ATPases and use ATP to move specific phospholipids including phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine from the outer to the cytosolic leaflet; floppases, which are ABC transporters using ATP to move phospholipids in the reverse direction; and scramblases, which move phospholipids bidirectionally and non-specifically without ATP, randomising the distribution.
claims.scope: Eukaryotic plasma membranes. Directions, ATP dependence and protein families are as reported by the cited reviews.
claims.uncertainty: Substrate specificities differ between individual transporters within each family, and the lesson does not name individual proteins beyond the family level.

claims.statement: Phosphatidylserine exposed on the outer surface of an activated platelet promotes blood clotting, and phosphatidylserine exposed on an apoptotic cell acts as an eat-me signal for macrophages.
claims.scope: Mammalian platelets and apoptotic cells. Used here to show that the maintained asymmetry exists so that abolishing it can carry information.
claims.uncertainty: Both are established signalling roles; the lesson makes no claim about their relative contribution in any tissue and states no clinical consequence.

claims.statement: The fluid mosaic model was set out in 1971 to 1972, and heterogeneity within membranes was already observed in the 1960s, so the word mosaic never carried a claim that membrane components are uniformly distributed.
claims.scope: The history and correct reading of the model, used to name the misconception this scene repairs.
claims.uncertainty: The review argues a position about how the model has been misread; the dates and the existence of 1960s heterogeneity evidence are the parts the lesson relies on.

claims.statement: The apical and basolateral membranes of intestinal epithelial cells are two biochemically and functionally distinct domains with different protein and lipid compositions: the apical membrane faces the lumen and both forms a defensive barrier against pathogens and processes and takes up nutrients, while the basolateral membrane handles interactions with adjacent cells and with the basement membrane, and the tight junction sits between the two domains.
claims.scope: Intestinal epithelial cells. This is the general polarity statement the lesson's enterocyte argument rests on.
claims.uncertainty: A general statement across intestinal epithelial cells; the lesson does not claim identical composition across segments of the gut.

claims.statement: Enterocyte brush border lipid is unusually rich in glycolipids, exceeding 30 per cent in the pig against about 5 per cent of total lipid in typical cell membranes; glycolipids together with cholesterol and sphingomyelin promote liquid-ordered microdomains in the outer leaflet, those of the brush border are thought to be relatively large and stable, and the organisation provides physical and chemical stability against luminal agents including bile salts, pancreatic digestive enzymes and pathogens.
claims.scope: Small-intestinal enterocyte brush border, with the quantitative glycolipid figure from pig. The lesson states both restrictions in the scene where the figures are used and does not assert the same numbers for the colonic absorptive cell.
claims.uncertainty: The lipid raft model of ordered microdomains remains under active discussion in the field, and domain size and stability are inferred rather than directly observed in intact tissue. The stability-against-lumen statement is the authors' functional interpretation of the composition.

claims.statement: Brush border microvilli are about 1 micrometre long with a radius of about 50 nanometres, thousands of them form the brush border, and the brush border provides roughly a 30-fold increase in apical surface area.
claims.scope: Intestinal brush border microvilli. Used for the scale comparison with a 5 nm membrane and as the distance in a diffusion practice task.
claims.uncertainty: Reported microvillus lengths span roughly 1 to 2 micrometres across studies and species, and the surface amplification factor varies with developmental stage and gut segment.

claims.statement: The tight junction acts as a diffusion barrier in the exoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane and not in the cytoplasmic leaflet: a fluorescent phospholipid delivered to the outer leaflet of the apical membrane of a Madin-Darby canine kidney monolayer did not move to the basolateral side, while the same marker delivered to both leaflets redistributed to the basolateral membrane immediately. Particular plasma-membrane enzymes and transport proteins are likewise confined to the apical or to the basal and lateral surfaces, and that separation of both protein and lipid is attributed at least in part to tight junctions.
claims.scope: Polarised epithelial monolayers. The lipid result is one labelled phospholipid in one canine kidney cell line, which the lesson states, and the protein confinement statement is the textbook generalisation.
claims.uncertainty: The experiment shows retention of an existing difference and says nothing about how proteins or lipids reach the correct face in the first place. The lesson makes that limit an explicit teaching point rather than leaving it implicit.

claims.statement: Phosphate-to-phosphate bilayer thickness measured by solution x-ray scattering on membranes purified from rat liver differs by compartment: apical plasma membrane 42.5 plus or minus 0.3 angstroms, basolateral plasma membrane 35.6 plus or minus 0.6, Golgi 39.5 plus or minus 0.4, endoplasmic reticulum 37.5 plus or minus 0.4. Cholesterol depletion changed thickness by at most 1 angstrom while protein removal changed it by 4 to 5, supporting the conclusion that membrane proteins rather than cholesterol modulate average bilayer thickness.
claims.scope: Membranes purified from rat liver. The apical membrane measured is a hepatocyte one rather than an intestinal brush border, and the lesson says so where the numbers are used.
claims.uncertainty: One study, one tissue, one technique. It establishes that the faces of a polarised cell can differ measurably in bilayer thickness; it does not establish the magnitude of that difference in any other cell type.

claims.statement: Amphotericin B interacts with ergosterol rather than targeting a specific enzyme. Two accounts of what follows are current: that polyenes interact with ergosterol to form ion-leaking pores in the membrane, and that the drug exists largely as extramembranous aggregates that extract ergosterol from the bilayer in a sterol sponge mechanism.
claims.scope: Mechanism of the polyene antifungals as summarised in a 2020 review. Presented as a teaching example about membrane composition, not as clinical guidance.
claims.uncertainty: The review states that the relative contribution of the pore and sponge mechanisms to antifungal activity remains to be established, and the lesson presents both accounts as current rather than choosing between them.

claims.statement: Amphotericin B binds ergosterol through van der Waals forces, a hydrogen bond network, and a pi-pi electronic interaction between the ergosterol side chain and the polyene tail; that last attachment point does not occur when the drug binds cholesterol. The higher ergosterol to phospholipid ratio in fungal cell membranes, compared with the cholesterol to phospholipid ratio in mammalian cells, also explains the selectivity.
claims.scope: The chemical and compositional bases of polyene selectivity as reported in a 2020 review. Used as a teaching example of how a composition difference between two membranes becomes a drug target.
claims.uncertainty: Binding models for polyene antifungals continue to be refined, and the relative weight of the chemical and compositional contributions to selectivity is not quantified in the source.

claims.statement: Despite roughly tenfold higher affinity for ergosterol, non-selective disruption of mammalian cell membranes by amphotericin B does occur. Nephrotoxicity is attributed to vasoconstriction in afferent renal arterioles, which decreases renal blood flow and glomerular filtration, and to increased cellular exposure through low-density-lipoprotein receptor mediated endocytosis; acute infusion reactions follow recognition by TLR2 and CD14 on mononuclear immune cells. Lipid formulations show less nephrotoxicity than the deoxycholate formulation, and the liposomal formulation also shows fewer infusion-related reactions.
claims.scope: Reported toxicity mechanisms and formulation comparison from a 2020 review, used only to show that a selectivity ratio is not a switch. No dose, threshold, indication, monitoring plan or recommendation is stated.
claims.uncertainty: Relative toxicity between formulations depends on the comparison and the population studied, and the review reports the direction rather than a magnitude the lesson could use. Nothing here is clinical guidance.

claims.statement: The commonest route to amphotericin B resistance is alteration of the sterol composition of the fungal cell membrane, with loss of function of the ERG11 and ERG3 genes leading to exchange of ergosterol for alternate sterols such as lanosterol, eburicol and 4,14-dimethyl-zymosterol.
claims.scope: Fungal resistance mechanisms as summarised in a 2020 review, used to close the lesson on the point that composition is the adjustable part of a membrane.
claims.uncertainty: Whether a resistant strain pays for its sterol substitution in altered membrane behaviour is not addressed by the source, and the lesson poses that as an open question rather than answering it.

terms.definition: A sheet exactly two lipid molecules thick that separates one space from another, behaves as a liquid within its own plane, and controls what crosses it. The everyday sense of a thin separating sheet, as in a drum skin or the film inside an eggshell, keeps only the separating part. The plasma membrane is the one enclosing the whole cell.

Two facing layers of lipid molecules with their water-avoiding tails buried between them and their water-attracting heads exposed to water on each side. It is the structural core of every biological membrane and is about 5 nanometres thick overall, with a water-avoiding interior of about 3 to 3.5 nanometres.

Having both a water-attracting and a water-avoiding part in the same molecule. A phospholipid is amphipathic: a phosphate-containing head that water accommodates, and two hydrocarbon tails that it does not.

The tendency of water-avoiding molecules in water to cluster together. Water must reorganise into ordered cage-like arrangements around such a molecule, which costs free energy, and the cost falls when the water-avoiding parts group so that fewer water molecules are affected. It is what assembles a bilayer and what holds one together, because no bond joins one lipid to its neighbour.

One of the two layers of lipid making up a bilayer. In a plasma membrane the outer or exoplasmic leaflet faces the space outside the cell and the inner or cytoplasmic leaflet faces the cytoplasm. The two hold different lipids, and this lesson treats that difference as one of the two main organising facts about membranes.

Movement of a lipid or protein within the plane of one leaflet, past its neighbours. It is fast: a lipid swaps places with a neighbour about ten million times a second, giving a diffusion coefficient near one square micrometre per second, so a lipid crosses a cell-sized distance in a couple of minutes.

Movement of a lipid from one leaflet of a bilayer to the other, which requires dragging its water-attracting head through the water-avoiding interior. Spontaneous flip-flop is rare, less than once a month per molecule in synthetic bilayers, and an established difference between the leaflets takes days to run down without enzymes.

A qualitative summary of how easily the hydrocarbon chains in a bilayer move and how loosely they pack. The measurable quantities behind the word are viscosity and chain order; this lesson uses it as a direction of travel rather than as a number, which is what the outcome asks a learner to predict.

The change of a bilayer between a liquid state, with chains bending and lipids sliding past one another, and a rigid crystalline state with the chains packed straight and parallel. The temperature at which it happens falls when chains are shorter or carry cis double bonds, and cholesterol obstructs the transition.

A small, rigid, largely water-avoiding molecule with one hydroxyl group, wedged among the hydrocarbon chains of animal membranes, where it can be up to 40 per cent of plasma-membrane lipid. It restricts chain movement in a fluid bilayer and also obstructs crystallisation, so it buffers a membrane against change rather than pushing fluidity in one direction, and it lowers permeability to small water-soluble molecules.

The homeostatic adjustment of membrane lipid composition that holds membrane viscosity roughly fixed as growth temperature changes, chiefly by varying the proportion of packing-disrupting chains such as unsaturated or branched ones and by varying chain length. The ability is broadly conserved across living things.

The maintained difference in composition between the two leaflets of a membrane. In a eukaryotic plasma membrane, phosphatidylcholine and the sphingolipids sit mainly outside while phosphatidylserine, phosphatidylethanolamine and the phosphoinositides are held inside. Slow flip-flop lets the difference persist; ATP-driven transporters create it.

A P4-ATPase that spends ATP to move specific phospholipids, phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine among them, from the outer leaflet to the cytoplasmic one. Flippases are what establish and maintain lipid asymmetry. A floppase is a different transporter, not another name for this one: it spends ATP to move lipids the opposite way, out to the outer leaflet, and generally belongs to the ABC transporter family.

A transporter that moves phospholipids in both directions across a bilayer without specificity and without ATP, randomising the distribution between the leaflets. Switching one on abolishes an asymmetry the cell has been paying to maintain, which is how exposed phosphatidylserine becomes a signal.

A protein embedded in the bilayer itself and not removable by gentle extraction that leaves the bilayer intact. Most cross it, and those are transmembrane proteins; some sit in one leaflet only, so transmembrane is the narrower word rather than a synonym. Integral proteins diffuse laterally and rotate about an axis across the membrane, and they do not flip-flop, so the side each part of the protein faces is fixed for its working life.

A protein attached to one face of a membrane through interactions with other proteins rather than embedded in the bilayer, and releasable by gentle treatments such as extreme pH or high or low salt that leave the bilayer intact.

The face of an epithelial cell that looks onto the lumen. In an intestinal absorptive cell it forms the brush border, carries an unusual lipid composition, and does the barrier and nutrient-uptake work.

The face of an epithelial cell that looks onto its neighbours and onto the basement membrane beneath the sheet. It carries a different set of lipids and proteins from the apical face of the same cell, and its business is contact with the tissue rather than with the lumen.

The apical specialisation of an absorptive intestinal cell: thousands of finger-like microvilli, each about a micrometre long and about a hundred nanometres across, raising apical surface area roughly thirtyfold. Its membrane is unusually rich in glycolipids, which with cholesterol and sphingomyelin form ordered domains that give it stability against the lumen. A single one of those projections is a microvillus; the brush border is the array and its associated structure, so the two words are not interchangeable.

A patch of membrane in which glycolipids, sphingomyelin and cholesterol pack more tightly and move less freely than the surrounding bilayer, while still remaining fluid. Such domains form in the outer leaflet and are unusually large and stable in the enterocyte brush border. The model of these domains remains under active discussion in the field.

The account of membrane structure set out in 1971 to 1972, in which proteins sit within and upon a fluid lipid bilayer and components diffuse within the plane. Mosaic never implied that components are evenly spread; uneven distribution within membranes was already being observed in the 1960s.

The sterol fungi build into their membranes where animal cells use cholesterol. It does the same structural job and is a different molecule, and that difference is what amphotericin B binds and what makes the drug more toxic to a fungus than to us.

Attribution and provenance

Lesson identity

Original contribution

The lesson prose, the two-faces diagram, the unit conversion and diffusion arithmetic, the crossing-time worked example and its recomputation at the slower in-cell coefficient, the order-of-magnitude comparison between lateral and transbilayer movement, the dial table, the two-organism prediction task, the disrupted-monolayer prediction task, the experimental-antifungal case in the assessment, all prompts, feedback, assessment items, rubrics, and glossary definitions were created for EmbeddedKnowledge and are contributed under CC BY 4.0 by the accountable principal.

Assets

Two figures appear in this pack.

  • assets/cell-membrane-components.svg is third party. It is the labelled cell membrane diagram by Mariana Ruiz, who publishes on Wikimedia Commons as LadyofHats, at the file page for File:Cell membrane detailed diagram en.svg. The licence was verified on the file's own page, which states that the work has been released into the public domain by its author and that anyone may use it for any purpose without conditions unless conditions are required by law. The source field records own work and the page names no upstream creator or organisation, so this is not a case of a third party's art mirrored onto Commons. The Commons API returns the same result for the same file: licence short name Public domain, usage terms Public domain, copyrighted False, attribution required false, artist Mariana Ruiz, credit Own work. The file is 877 by 361 pixels, an aspect ratio near 2.4 to 1, which sits inside the landscape band this project prefers for a guided frame; aspect ratio was checked before the licence, as the illustration rules direct. Three modifications were made and are declared in lesson.json: the XML prolog and generator comment were removed, the DOCTYPE was removed, and title and desc accessibility elements were added. The artwork itself is unchanged. The file was scanned before use and contains no script, style, use, image, foreignObject, href, external reference, or data URI. Displayed attribution: Cell membrane detailed diagram by Mariana Ruiz (LadyofHats), released into the public domain.
  • diagrams/enterocyte-two-faces.diagram.json is original work created for this lesson. Its nodes, its edges, its alt text, and its long description were written here from the numbers this pack's own sources supply. It is declared in originalAssets.

The third-party figure has one visible flaw worth recording: its label reads Peripherial protein, which is a spelling slip for peripheral. The prose spells the term correctly and the figure's long description uses the correct spelling. Nothing else on the figure is wrong, and correcting the label would mean redrawing artwork this pack has no reason to redraw.

That figure also draws the same lipid on both leaflets, which is a limit of what a static inventory diagram can show. The lesson names that limit where the figure appears and again in the fourth scene, where leaflet asymmetry is taught. The two-faces diagram exists because no correctly licensed third-party figure this pack found makes the apical-against-basolateral argument the fifth scene needs.

No Servier Medical Art asset appears in this pack, and no request was made to smart.servier.com during this authoring run.

No other image, media file, or dataset appears in the pack, and the lesson ships no third-party expression.

Terminology continuity

The course terminology ledger was read before the glossary was designed. Every one of the twenty-two entries introduces a term no published lesson currently owns, so no alignment block was required. The ledger matches on the term string, and the entries closest to an existing one are checked below.

  • liquid-ordered domain does not collide with domain, which PREM-QNT-005 and PREM-QNT-007 own in a mathematical sense. The alias ordered domain is used rather than the bare word, so no ledger match arises and no mathematical sense is displaced.
  • membrane fluidity and lateral diffusion are new to the corpus. The glossary states plainly that fluidity is used qualitatively here and that the measurable quantities behind it are viscosity and chain order.
  • membrane arrives loaded from everyday English, which the block brief flags. The collision is named once in the first scene, where the ordinary sense of a thin separating sheet is kept and the three things the biological sense adds are stated.
  • cell, tissue, epithelium and stem cell are owned by PREM-BIO-001 and are used here in that lesson's sense without being redefined, so they carry no glossary entry in this pack.

Source use and rights

Fifteen sources support the factual claims. Every one was used for facts only, followed by an independent instructional structure and original expression; no source is quoted, adapted, redrawn, or reorganised anywhere in the pack, and no example, question, table, figure, or dataset is taken from any of them. Complete locators, use records, rights evidence, and dated agent-access checks appear in references.json.

  • source-alberts-lipid-bilayer, Alberts and colleagues, Molecular Biology of the Cell, chapter on the lipid bilayer: water-driven assembly and the free-energy cost of ordering water around a hydrophobic molecule; the impossibility of a free edge and the spontaneous closure of a tear; about 5 × 10^6 lipid molecules per square micrometre and about 10^9 in a small animal cell's plasma membrane; the two-dimensional-fluid description; exchange with a neighbour about 10^7 times per second, a lateral diffusion coefficient near 10^-8 cm²/s, and about 2 µm per second; flip-flop less than once a month in synthetic bilayers; the phase transition and its lowering by short chains and cis double bonds; cholesterol's two effects and its reduction of permeability to small water-soluble molecules; the leaflet distribution of the phospholipid classes.
  • source-alberts-membrane-proteins, the same textbook's chapter on membrane proteins: protein at about 50 per cent of a typical plasma membrane's mass, below 25 per cent in myelin and about 75 per cent in ATP-producing membranes; the distinction between proteins embedded in the bilayer and peripheral proteins releasable by gentle extraction; rotation and lateral diffusion of membrane proteins without flip-flop, and the mouse-and-human heterokaryon in which the two sets of surface proteins mixed across the whole surface within about half an hour; confinement of particular plasma-membrane enzymes and transporters to the apical or to the basal and lateral surfaces, attributed at least in part to tight junctions.
  • source-bickerton-bilayer-thickness, Bickerton, Johnson, Kerckhoffs and Langton: overall membrane thickness of about 5 to 5.5 nm including the head groups, with a hydrophobic interior of about 3 to 3.5 nm. This is the source behind the block's canonical 5 nm figure as used here.
  • source-bernardino-plasma-membrane, Bernardino de la Serna, Schütz, Eggeling and Cebecauer: sterols up to 40 per cent of plasma-membrane lipid and hundreds to thousands of phospholipid species; lipid tracers diffusing about four times faster in model membranes than in living-cell plasma membranes; the 1971 to 1972 date of the fluid mosaic model and 1960s evidence of membrane heterogeneity.
  • source-galbraith-resolution-limit, Galbraith and Galbraith: the roughly 250 nm lateral resolution limit of conventional light microscopy. PREM-BIO-001 established the same figure from the same source; it was re-verified for this pack.
  • source-segawa-flippases, Segawa, Suzuki and Nagata: the leaflet distribution of the phospholipid classes; ATP-dependent flippases and ATP-independent scramblases; a half-time of several days for an established asymmetry to decay without enzymatic help; phosphatidylserine exposure promoting clotting on activated platelets and acting as an eat-me signal on apoptotic cells.
  • source-hankins-flippases, Hankins, Baldridge, Xu and Graham: the three-family scheme of P4-ATPase flippases, ABC-transporter floppases and ATP-independent scramblases, their directions, and the restriction of phosphatidylserine, phosphatidylethanolamine and the phosphoinositides to the cytosolic leaflet.
  • source-hoogerland-homeoviscous, Hoogerland, van den Berg, Suo and colleagues: the definition of homeoviscous adaptation; the compositional strategies of unsaturation, branching and chain length; the broad conservation of the trait; and the growth defect and rescue of an Escherichia coli strain unable to make the required lipid. The lesson presents that experiment as bacterial.
  • source-vanmeer-tight-junction, van Meer and Simons: the liposome-fusion experiment in a polarised kidney monolayer, both conditions, both results, and the conclusion that the tight junction is a diffusion barrier in the exoplasmic leaflet and not in the cytoplasmic one.
  • source-danielsen-brush-border, Danielsen and Hansen: brush border glycolipids exceeding 30 per cent in pig against about 5 per cent in typical cell membranes; liquid-ordered domains formed by glycolipids with cholesterol and sphingomyelin in the outer leaflet; and the stability that organisation gives against bile salts, pancreatic digestive enzymes and pathogens in the lumen.
  • source-brown-microvillar, Brown and McKnight: microvilli about 1 µm long with a radius of about 50 nm, thousands per brush border, and a roughly 30-fold increase in apical surface area.
  • source-mitra-bilayer-thickness, Mitra, Ubarretxena-Belandia, Taguchi, Warren and Engelman: phosphate-to-phosphate bilayer thicknesses of 42.5 Å apical, 35.6 Å basolateral, 39.5 Å Golgi and 37.5 Å endoplasmic reticulum in rat liver membranes, with protein rather than cholesterol accounting for the modulation. The lesson states that these are hepatocyte measurements.
  • source-schneeberger-polarity, Schneeberger, Roth, Nieuwenhuis and Middendorp: apical and basolateral membranes as biochemically and functionally distinct domains with different protein and lipid compositions; what each faces and does; and the position of the tight junction between them.
  • source-carolus-amphotericin, Carolus, Pierson, Lagrou and Van Dijck: the drug's interaction with ergosterol; the pore and sterol-sponge accounts; the three binding interactions and the attachment point absent with cholesterol; the sterol-to-phospholipid ratio basis of selectivity; the tenfold affinity preference alongside continuing non-selective disruption of mammalian membranes; the described contributions to kidney toxicity and to infusion reactions; the toxicity difference between formulations; and resistance through altered fungal sterol composition.
  • source-nguyen-colonic-crypt, Nguyen, Lausten and Boman: the crypt context carried forward from PREM-BIO-001, including upward migration with differentiation, replacement of absorptive cells every four to five days, and the barrier role of the epithelium.

Several of these sources retain publisher copyright and one is a public-access author manuscript. None supplies any expression, figure, table, dataset, or example to this pack; all are used strictly as evidence for facts, which is the basis recorded in references.json for every source here.

Adjudication repairs to the 0.1.0 candidate

The academic review returned request-changes with five major and three minor findings; the learning-design review approved with five notes. All eight were repaired in one finalization pass and none was declined.

Three of the majors were answer keys that required a false argument to score full marks, which is the worst kind of defect this corpus can ship: a learner who reasons correctly loses the point.

  • A dose argument had the direction of saturation backwards. The key said that raising the dose leaves the ratio between fungal and human effect roughly unchanged while the absolute effect rises. Binding saturates, so the preferred target fills first and the margin narrows as the dose climbs; a thirtyfold advantage is largest at low occupancy and worth nothing once both sterols are saturated. The fixed-ratio version is the reassuring form of the very error the item was built to catch. The key now also credits the deeper answer, that an affinity ratio is not an effect ratio without exposure, sterol abundance, stoichiometry and response.

  • An intervention that hits everything was treated as though it isolated one thing. The key required the answer that interrupting ATP for several hours leaves both separations intact. Half of that holds: stopping the flippases alone would remove little of the leaflet asymmetry, because what preserves it is the slowness of spontaneous crossing rather than the pumps. The other half does not, because removing ATP also removes it from the cytoskeleton the junction is anchored to, and this lesson's sources say nothing about what a general energy failure does to the fence. The item now asks what the experiment would and would not establish, and credits a learner who proposes a better-aimed one. It is a better question than the one it replaced.

  • A correction was required twice on a number that already contained it. The stem stipulates D = 2 µm²/s, which sits inside the 0.5 to 4 range measured in living cell membranes, so the key's demand that crowding makes the answer an underestimate double-counted the crowding. Part (d) now asks the learner to notice that, and to name something the relation does not represent at all — the tight-junction fence from scene 5, which stops the journey rather than slowing it. That ties the arithmetic scene to the polarity scene, which the item previously did not.

  • The two accounts of amphotericin B were collapsed into one destination. The scene said the disagreement was over the route and not the destination. In the pore account the sterol stays in the membrane as part of an ion-conducting structure; only the sponge account ends in a sterol-depleted membrane. Both predict a membrane that leaks, which is why the outcome alone has not settled the question, and the scene now says that instead. The sterol-removal predictions are attributed to the branch that supports them.

  • Scene 5 contradicted itself. It stated that the two faces are continuous around the top of the cell, then called them two membranes rather than two regions of one. Apical and basolateral are domains of a single plasma membrane. The 7 Å thickness difference demonstrates that the domains are structurally different, which is the stronger and the true claim, and the heading and the argument now say that.

  • Three glossary corrections: a floppase is a different transporter and not another name for a flippase; a microvillus is one projection and the brush border is the array; and transmembrane is the narrower word rather than a synonym for integral, since some integral proteins sit in one leaflet only.

Worth recording about all three glossary findings and the amphotericin one: the claim ledger was already correct in each case. claim-flippase-scramblase separates the three transporter families, claim-microvillus-dimensions says thousands of microvilli form the brush border, and claim-amphotericin-target states the two mechanisms distinctly. The defect each time was in the teaching surface drifting from a ledger that had it right, not in the sourcing. That is a different failure from an unsupported claim and it needs a different check: reading the prose against the ledger rather than against the source.
